interactions.label: Which adhesion structures anchor the epidermis to the underlying basement membra

params.question: Which adhesion structures anchor the epidermis to the underlying basement membrane?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Desmosomes and their desmogleins hold keratinocytes to each other within the epidermis, not to the basement membrane. Loss of desmoglein function causes intra-epidermal splitting, as seen in pemphigus.

Correct. Hemidesmosomes, with their key proteins BP180 and BP230, anchor basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane zone. Autoantibodies against these proteins cause the sub-epidermal split in bullous pemphigoid.
Tight junctions contribute to the epidermal barrier in the granular layer but are not the primary structures anchoring the epidermis to the dermis. That anchoring role belongs to hemidesmosomes.
Gap junctions allow intercellular communication but do not provide structural adhesion between the epidermis and dermis. Hemidesmosomes serve this anchoring function.

overallFeedback.feedback: Hemidesmosomes, containing BP180 and BP230, anchor the epidermis to the basement membrane. Remember: desmosomes hold keratinocytes to each other (intra-epidermal glue), while hemidesmosomes hold the epidermis down to the dermis (dermo-epidermal junction).
Well done. Hemidesmosomes with BP180 and BP230 form the critical attachment between epidermis and dermis — they are the precise targets in bullous pemphigoid.

params.question: Why does pemphigus vulgaris commonly present with oral erosions before skin involvement?

answers.text: The oral mucosa has a thinner stratum corneum that ruptures more easily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the oral mucosa does lack a thick cornified layer, the reason PV starts there is the abundance of its target antigen. Thinness alone does not explain the specific autoimmune targeting of oral keratinocytes.

answers.text: Desmoglein 3, the target antigen in PV, is particularly abundant in the oral mucosa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Desmoglein 3 is highly expressed in the oral epithelium. Since IgG autoantibodies in PV target Dsg3, the oral mucosa is attacked earliest and most severely, producing painful non-healing erosions weeks before skin blisters appear.

answers.text: The oral mucosa lacks hemidesmosomes and is therefore structurally weaker

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The oral mucosa does possess hemidesmosomes anchoring epithelium to the basement membrane. PV targets desmoglein 3 in desmosomes (cell-to-cell adhesion), not hemidesmosomes — the oral predilection is due to the high concentration of Dsg3 there.

answers.text: Complement activation is stronger in mucosal tissue than in skin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complement activation plays a more prominent role in bullous pemphigoid (sub-epidermal), not primarily in pemphigus. PV causes acantholysis mainly through direct antibody-mediated disruption of desmoglein 3, which is most abundant in the oral mucosa.

overallFeedback.feedback: Pemphigus vulgaris often begins in the mouth because its target protein, desmoglein 3, is highly concentrated in the oral mucosa. Anti-Dsg3 antibodies therefore disrupt oral keratinocyte adhesion earliest, producing persistent painful erosions.
Exactly right. The abundance of desmoglein 3 in the oral epithelium makes the mouth the first and most severely affected site in pemphigus vulgaris.

interactions.label: Nikolsky's sign is positive in bullous pemphigoid because the large, tense blist

params.question: Nikolsky's sign is positive in bullous pemphigoid because the large, tense blisters indicate significant epidermal damage.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Nikolsky's sign is actually negative in bullous pemphigoid. Although the blisters are large, they are tense precisely because the epidermis is intact and cohesive — the split is sub-epidermal. Nikolsky's sign tests whether keratinocytes separate from each other (intra-epidermal fragility), which occurs in pemphigus, not pemphigoid.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well reasoned. Nikolsky's sign is negative in bullous pemphigoid because the autoantibodies target the dermo-epidermal junction (BP180/BP230), not the inter-keratinocyte adhesion. The epidermis itself remains intact and cohesive, which is precisely why the bullae are tense — they have a thick, full-thickness epidermal roof that resists shearing.

params.question: When confirming a suspected autoimmune blistering disease, biopsies are taken from two separate sites. What is the specific purpose of the sample taken from normal-looking perilesional skin?

answers.text: To culture for bacterial superinfection of the surrounding skin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bacterial culture is done separately when clinically indicated. The perilesional biopsy is specifically for direct immunofluorescence, which detects the pattern of immunoglobulin and complement deposition that distinguishes between different autoimmune blistering diseases.

answers.text: To assess the degree of dermal inflammation and eosinophil infiltration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dermal inflammation and eosinophil infiltration are assessed on the lesional biopsy sent for routine histology. The perilesional sample serves a different purpose — direct immunofluorescence to identify the specific pattern of immune deposits.

answers.text: To perform direct immunofluorescence, revealing the pattern of antibody and complement deposition that distinguishes different blistering diseases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Direct immunofluorescence on perilesional skin is the gold standard for differentiating autoimmune blistering diseases. Pemphigus shows intercellular (fish-net) IgG/C3 deposition, while bullous pemphigoid shows a linear band of IgG/C3 along the basement membrane zone.

answers.text: To compare normal histological architecture with the lesional sample for disease staging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Disease staging is not the purpose of the second biopsy. The perilesional sample undergoes direct immunofluorescence — a specialised immunological test that maps where antibodies and complement deposit in relation to the basement membrane and the intercellular spaces of the epidermis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The perilesional sample is sent for direct immunofluorescence (DIF), the gold standard test. It detects immune deposits in a characteristic pattern: fish-net intercellular IgG/C3 in pemphigus, or linear basement-membrane IgG/C3 in bullous pemphigoid.

Precisely right. The perilesional biopsy for DIF is the gold standard — it reveals intercellular fish-net IgG in pemphigus versus linear basement-membrane IgG in bullous pemphigoid, giving the definitive distinction.

params.question: A 78-year-old patient is diagnosed with bullous pemphigoid affecting the trunk and limbs. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment approach?

answers.text: High-dose oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg/day combined with azathioprine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This aggressive regimen is reserved for pemphigus vulgaris, not bullous pemphigoid. In frail elderly patients, high-dose systemic corticosteroids carry substantial risks including infection, diabetes, and osteoporosis. BP typically responds to less aggressive therapy.

answers.text: Potent topical corticosteroids applied to the affected areas

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Bullous pemphigoid, especially in elderly patients, often responds well to potent topical corticosteroids as initial treatment. This avoids the serious systemic side effects of high-dose oral steroids, which are particularly dangerous in frail older patients.

Rituximab is a specialist-level option used in moderate to severe pemphigus vulgaris or refractory cases. It is not first-line treatment for bullous pemphigoid, which typically responds to less aggressive topical or low-dose systemic therapy.

answers.text: Oral dapsone as sole therapy without any corticosteroid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dapsone alone is not the standard first-line approach for bullous pemphigoid. Potent topical or systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay. For mild localised BP, doxycycline with nicotinamide is a recognised alternative, but dapsone monotherapy is not the established protocol.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bullous pemphigoid in elderly patients is typically managed initially with potent topical corticosteroids, avoiding the significant side effects of high-dose systemic steroids. Reserve aggressive multi-agent immunosuppression (prednisolone + azathioprine/rituximab) for pemphigus vulgaris.
Well done. Potent topical corticosteroids are often sufficient for bullous pemphigoid and are especially appropriate in elderly patients, where systemic immunosuppression carries greater risk.
